en: *Record of Elucidating the Profound Meaning of the Treatise on the Original Person* (with preface),
composed by the Śramaṇa Jingyuan of Jinshui.
In the second year following the change of the reign title to Zhiping, the Great Master Keyong of Chongyin in Hangzhou, taking the *Treatise on the Original Person* and...
He presented a table of contents as a formal gift and requested that I examine it, saying that he might perhaps compose a commentary upon it.

As I reflected on the composition of this treatise, I considered that its purpose was to refute the superficiality of the two teachings [Confucianism and Daoism] and to harmonize the profound mysteries of the One Vehicle. Therefore, its doctrinal principles all employ the words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;

it does not use the terminology of Confucianism or Daoism to form its literary style. This is not the work of one who has not studied deeply, mastered antiquity, and thoroughly penetrated the depths of Zhongni’s [Confucius’s] thought.
To establish a model for posterity, one who thoroughly investigates the words of Laozi (Boyang) finds themselves at a loss as to what to hold dear.
Were it not so, how could one provide for the descendants of future generations, ensuring that they pass down the Way and its Virtue shoulder to shoulder and step after step?

(Yuan) In the past, I once read the extensive *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué shùchāo*), and within it, specifically the chapter that exhaustively analyzes the myriad phenomena to deduce the single mind, there was only a brilliant and authentic exposition.
To resolve doubts and clear obstructions, the details are set forth in the *Commentary* (*Chao*), as clear as pointing at one's own palm.
Therefore, I have not hesitated to compile this *Record of Dispelling Obscurity* to expand upon the essential terms of the *Commentary* and to elucidate the subtle purport of this treatise.

It is my hope that the profound texts and esoteric meanings of our Patriarch will not fall into ruin, and that the intentions of those who requested this work will likewise be fully realized. Having recorded the words of the Master of the Commentary, I thereby seek to reveal their subtle significance.
Therefore, it is titled the *Fawei lu* (Record of Elucidating the Subtle).
It was written on the eleventh day of the eighth month in the year of Jiayin, during the sixth reign of the Sacred Song dynasty, at the Xianshou Teaching Institute in Qiantang.
Preface to the *Yuanren lun* (Treatise on the Origin of Man), including the preface.

Regarding the title *Yuanren lun*: "yuan" (origin) means to investigate thoroughly and to exhaustively examine. It refers to extensively investigating both internal [Buddhist] and external [non-Buddhist] teachings to trace back and exhaustively analyze the myriad phenomena.
The *Fayuan* traces the origin of humanity to taking the single mind as its foundation. There are two explanations for the character "ren" (human):

first, "much thought" (*duo-si*); second, "much grace" (*duo-en*). The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that it is because of much thought that one is able to deliberate upon good and evil, thereby distinguishing oneself from other realms of existence.
As for "much grace," it refers to possessing the virtue of compassionate grace, which likewise distinguishes one from other realms of existence. Thus says the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā*.
That which is superior to all things and remains unchanged from beginning to end is called "human wisdom" (*puruṣajñāna*). The *Śāstra* states that one practices human dharmas;
thus, the interlocutors' questions and answers analyze and investigate [the meaning] to provide an exposition within the study of wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*).

Therefore, the subsequent sections—which refute provisional teachings, disparage shallow views, and reconcile partiality by returning to the Perfect—constitute precisely such analysis and investigation. As for the inclusion of the preface, it is because the title of the treatise encompasses the author's own introduction.
Therefore, it is called "the Preface" (*bingxu*). "Preface" (*xu*) means "to unfold" (*shu*); it unfolds and describes the relative depth of the Three Teachings and the sequence of the four chapters.

If one correlates "Preface" (*xu*) with "Treatise on the Original Man" (*yuanren lun*), two pairs are present: "Preface" is the "enabler of the description" (*nengxu*), while the first three characters [of the title] are the "object described" (*souxu*).
Thus, the "enabler of the description" corresponds to the "Treatise" (*lun*) as the "enabler of expression" (*nengquan*), and "Original Man" (*yuanren*) is the "object expressed" (*souxuan*).
*The Exposition on the Relationship Between the Expressor and the Expressed*, composed by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Mount Gui Peak at Caotang Monastery in Zhongnan. Regarding "Zhongnan":
it lies eight thousand *li* south of the imperial capital, where thousands of overlapping ridges and ten-thousand-fathom precipices rise in succession.
It lies at the southern extremity, reaching as far as the corner of the South Sea; hence it is called Zhongnan.
According to the *Shiming*, "shan" (mountain) means "to produce," for mountains produce all things.

As for Caotang, it originated when Kumārajīva constructed a hall within the Great Monastery and thatched its roof with grass (the character *shi* is pronounced *lián* and is also a type of grass) to translate various sutras and śāstras; thus, the name Caotang first arose during the Qin dynasty.
As for "Shi" (Śīla), "Gui-feng" (Jade-Tablet Peak) refers to this peak’s topographical form, which resembles a jade tablet (*gui*), hence its name.

"Lan-ruo" (Aranya) is translated as "free from clamor and dispute. "Sha-men" (Śramaṇa) is translated as "one who exerts effort and seeks rest"; it is a general title for those who have left the household life.
The subsequent individual names are specific appellations. Furthermore, because in India the act of naming is held in high esteem, personal names often include additional elements.
Regarding one's parents, later generations in the Middle Kingdom honor them by avoiding their names out of respect;

once the parents have passed away, hearing their names causes the heart to be startled and grieved (the character *jù* is pronounced *jù*, meaning "startled" or "grieved"). Therefore, people avoid their names.

However, one does not avoid the name within the ancestral temple, nor does one avoid it when composing formal texts. According to the *Preface to the Compendium of the Dharma* (composed by Pei Xiu), it says: "When Chan Master Zongmi of Guifeng was born..."

In Xichong, he mastered the Confucian classics; in Suining, having completed his studies, he was about to follow the system of recommendations to present himself to the authorities when he encountered the monk Daoyuan of Great Virtue.
Daoyuan had received the Dharma from Nanyin (the Chan Master Zhang of Jingnan), who was the direct descendant of the Great Master Heze in Chengdu.
Daoyuan was then teaching at Dayun Temple in Suzhou. The Chan Master [Wuxiang] traveled to Daoyuan’s seat and was ordained under him.

Xue became a disciple and received the teachings on the Mind. Later, while following the assembly of monks for a meal at the home of Ren Guan, a local official, he took his place among the lower ranks to receive the scriptures in order.
Upon reaching the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, he attained realization of its definitive meaning; before the chapter was finished, he was moved to tears of inspiration.
Returning home, he informed his teacher of what he had realized. His teacher patted him on the back and said, "You shall greatly propagate the teaching of the Perfect and Sudden."
"This sutra has been entrusted to you by all the Buddhas; go forth and do not remain stagnant in one corner. The Chan Master bowed his head and accepted the command.
Upon arriving in the region of Xianghan, he encountered someone from the capital carrying the Great Master Yunhua’s commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Having read it once, the Chan Master ascended the seat and lectured upon it; those who listened numbered in the thousands.
People from far and near were greatly astonished; he then proceeded to the capital and visited Yunhua Temple, where he performed the rites of a disciple.
He traveled north to Mount Qingliang and subsequently resided at Caotang Temple in Hu County. Before long, he entered Guishan to the south of the temple.
Wherever he went, both monastics and laypeople sought refuge in him like a bustling marketplace, and several hundred people attained the Dharma. He composed the *Yuan*... [text truncated]

He composed commentaries on the *Awakening of Faith*, the two versions of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* (the Great and Small), the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the *Catuḥprakaraṇa*, and the *Dharmadhātudarśana*.
(As traditional scholars have noted, such annotated commentaries are termed "chapters and sentences. Since then, this teaching of the Perfect and Sudden has widely circulated in the world.
Furthermore, his works on the fundamental source of the human way and the reconciliation of the differences within the Chan school responded to inquiries as they arose, awaiting all seekers.
Some were composed as answers to questions; others were written down because his followers were in distant lands and required instruction;
some were verses expounded to provide peace of mind for disciples at the end of their lives; some were declarations of the state of realization to encourage beginners;
and others were songs of the Way’s essence, sung while reclining upon the mountains where he dwelt. These writings are extensive and their principles are profoundly unified.
His words were concise yet their meaning was profoundly perfect; his disciples collected and compiled them into several chapters, forming ten volumes—a brilliant mirror of clarity and wisdom.
The Chan Master took the Dharma-realm as his inner sanctum, the scriptural teachings as his courtyard, compassion as his canopy, and sentient beings as his grove, praising them all day long.
I have related this without ever having given thought to literary composition;

what is now being transmitted is like the people of Mount Jing who used jade to strike at magpies (the *Yantie lun* states that "the people of Mount Jing used jade to strike at magpies," meaning their jade was so abundant they did not treasure it; "strike" means to hit).

Yet, it became something treasured by travelers (travelers who obtained it passed it on as a treasure; this is a metaphor for my teacher having already reached the place of treasure: whatever words he utters or points toward are nothing but wondrous gates, which his disciples themselves treasure).

I have merely lamented this. For a long time now, I have rested my head high upon the threshold and windows of my Master’s dwelling. (Because the teaching of my Master is perfect and sudden, illuminating the subtle and profound;

by entering its threshold and windows, one immediately becomes free from the anxiety of delusive attachments—hence the phrase "resting with the head high. If those who know were not to speak, how could later generations look up to the Way of my Master?
Therefore, I have roughly set forth its major points to serve as the preface to this collection. The above is the Preface to the *Dharma Collection*.
Later generations, lacking sufficient knowledge, have either placed [the preface] before the *Xingyuan chao* or prefixed it to the beginning of this treatise;

this is highly contrary to the subject matter of the discourse (for that preface concerns the *Dharmasaṃgraha*, not the *Yuanren lun*). I have now recorded it here within this collection solely to clarify the deeds and practices of the Master of the Treatise.
The commentator Paramārtha stated: "The Buddha spoke the sūtras; the Bodhisattvas composed the treatises."
I have directly set forth the Buddhist scriptures as a narrative, much like Zhongni (Confucius), who "narrated but did not compose.
The myriad spirits, though they seem inert, all possess their origin; the myriad things, though they flourish profusely, each returns to its root.
There has never been a case where there were branches and tips without a fundamental root.
"Ten thousand spirits" (*wanling*) refers to those that move; "spirits" (*ling*) means those possessing spirit, which is to say sentient beings as their primary retribution (*zhengbao*).
The *Renwang jing* states: "Sentient beings move about like mere illusions, merely dwelling [in the world]. As for the term "ten thousand," it is used here as a large number. The *Xinji* says:
"On land, in the air, in water, and on earth, the names and numbers of moving creatures and sentient beings are as numerous as motes of dust in a sunbeam; how could they be limited to ten thousand?"
"All have their root" means that even the crawling, wriggling, flying, and those born from wombs, eggs, moisture, or transformation all take the True Realm as their source.

The rootless branches below return to the clarity of the dependent and the primary; one takes the single mind as the root.
How much more so for that which is most spiritual among the Three Powers—how could it lack a source?

The word "kuàng" (況) means "shèn" (矧), which implies comparison. Now, even that which is subtle among the primary and secondary [aspects of reality] still possesses a fundamental basis for comparison with the Three Powers (sān cái).

Since only man is most spiritually gifted, how could he lack an original source? Regarding these Three Powers, the *Wénxīn diáolóng* states: "Looking upward, one observes the radiance emitted [Heavenly Talent];
looking downward, one examines the contained patterns [Earthly Talent]. Because high and low are established in their respective positions, they are called the Two Polarities."

The patterns [of Heaven and Earth] are already two; it is only Man who participates in them. That which the spiritual intelligence takes as its foundation is called the "Three Powers" (the Three Sages).

Furthermore, to know others is wisdom, but to know oneself is clarity. Now that I have received this human body, if I do not know from whence it has come, how can I know where I shall go in future lives?
How can I know the affairs of people throughout the past and present of the world?
Furthermore, the word "hu" (乎) is a particle. The passage "He who knows others is wise; he who knows himself is enlightened" is also from the *Daodejing*; Wang Bi’s commentary states:
"He who knows others merely possesses wisdom, yet this does not compare to he who knows himself, who transcends the realm of wisdom."
The Emperor said: "The wise employ their faculties to know things; the enlightened fuse their illumination to discern the subtle.
Where the wise have something they do not know, the enlightened have nothing they do not illuminate. To 'receive' (禀受) is simply the past; 'other lives' (他世) is simply the future.
Why is this? It is because of 'tending toward' (趣向). If one does not know oneself [in the present], how can one know the causes of the past?"
To know where one is headed in the future throughout the world is to understand the present, the past, and the future across the three periods of time.
Therefore, for several decades he studied without a fixed teacher, extensively examining both internal and external teachings to trace back to his own person.
By tracing it back without ceasing, he finally attained its fundamental source.
The phrase "learning has no constant teacher" appears in the *Analects*. Ma Rong’s commentary states: "Because one learns from everyone without exception, there is no constant teacher.

Furthermore, the *Book of Documents* says: "Virtue has no constant teacher; that which takes goodness as its master is the teacher. To "broadly examine" (博考) the internal and external means that "broad" (*bo*) refers to being extensive, and "examine" (*kao*) refers to investigation.

That which governs what lies outside the realm is called the "internal teaching" (*neijiao*); that which governs within the realm... [is called the external]. (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the extant portion.)
Regarding the self, this is what is called the "external teaching," which has already ceased; it is merely the fruit of past karma.
Yet those who today study Confucianism and Daoism know only the immediate: that this body was received through the continuous transmission from their ancestors and fathers.

"Practitioner" (*xi*) means "to learn"; "standard-bearer" (*ze*) is a term used to carry forward what precedes it; "ancestor" (*zu*)—in the *Zhengyi* (Correct Meaning) of the *Jifa* (Ritual Laws of Ancestral Worship)—is explained as "the beginning," meaning he is the origin of moral cultivation.
Regarding "father" (*fu*), the *Baitong* (White Tiger General Discourse) states: "A father is a 'model' (*ju*); he instructs his son by means of laws and measures.
As for "transmitting the physical body in succession," this means that the father transmits the inherited physical essence of the ancestor, continuing it without interruption.

It is absolute. The *Lanpen shu* (Commentary on the Ullambana Sūtra) states: "The traditions followed by those outside our teachings take physical form as their basis for the transmission of the essence and its continuity.
At a distance, the single qi of Chaos was divided into the two of Yin and Yang; from these two arose the three of Heaven, Earth, and Humanity; and from these three arose..."
The myriad things and all people have *qi* as their fundamental substance.
This undifferentiated, chaotic unity of *qi* is what is called "one," for at this stage, yin and yang have not yet been distinguished and the clear and the turbid are in harmonious union.

As Laozi said: "One cannot see it when looking at it; one cannot hear it when listening to it; one cannot grasp it when seizing it; it is impossible to question it further. Therefore, it is called "one."

"Blending into one" (the phrase "pounding with the hands" refers to striking together); "dividing into the two of yin and yang" means splitting apart—that is, the single qi first divides into the two qi of yin and yang.
"The two produce the three of heaven, earth, and humanity": the yang qi, being light and clear, becomes heaven;
the yin qi, being heavy and turbid, becomes earth; the harmonious and balanced qi (*chonghe*) becomes humanity. "The three produce the myriad things."

It is said that only when the Three Powers (Heaven, Earth, and Humanity) are complete do the myriad things come into being; both the myriad things and human beings take *qi* as their fundamental substance.

Those who study the Buddha-dharma merely say that, in the near term, one receives this human body by receiving retribution according to the karma created in a previous life.

The statement that "one receives retribution according to the karma created in previous lives" is merely a conventional expression; for karma is either good or evil, and its retribution is either suffering or joy.
Since this is the joyful retribution of good karma, it is said that one has obtained this human body (this introduces the teaching on humans and devas below).
As for "remote," it means that karma further induces [rebirth] through a succession of causes until the *ālaya-vijñāna* becomes the root of the body.
Regarding "karma further induces," this traces back to the fact that karma arises from greed, hatred, and delusion (this introduces the teaching of the Hīnayāna).
Regarding the *ālaya-vijñāna*, this traces back to the three poisons and the grasping at a self, which arise from the fundamental consciousness and the grasping at phenomena (this introduces...).

Regarding the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* (the teaching on the characteristics of phenomena), it does not include the "refutation of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-vināśa*) because this teaching implicitly reveals the principle of the true nature’s emptiness and quiescence; therefore, it is not included therein.
As for the teachings that reveal the nature (*prakṛti-prakāśana*), they are situated within the category of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
All claim to have exhausted the principles [of their respective systems], yet in reality they have not.

Regarding the phrase "all claim to have exhausted," those who study Confucianism and Daoism take the vital breath (*qi*) as fundamental, while those who study the Buddha-dharma take consciousness (*vijñāna*) as fundamental;
they merely say they have exhausted this physical body, yet in truth they have not reached the ultimate source.

However, Confucius, Laozi, and Śākyamuni are all supreme sages who, responding to the times and adapting to beings, established teachings through diverse paths; internal and external traditions complement one another to benefit the masses.

through their virtue, people turned toward them with benevolence, and they flourished as a powerful nation. The father-king later felt regret and dispatched an envoy to summon his four sons, but they declined the invitation and did not return.

According to the *Jingzheng fahang jing* (Sūtra on the Pure Dharma Practice), the Tathāgata first dispatched three sages to transform China—Laozi being Mahākāśyapa and Zhongni being the Youth Pure Light.
Those who respond to beings according to the times each act in accordance with the capacities of beings at that particular time. As for those who establish teachings through diverse paths:

"What has come from? refers to that which has never been cultivated or contemplated; "contemplated" (*lù*) here refers to the mental states of love, hatred, joy, and anger.
If one were to say that things arise spontaneously without the seeds of past-life cultivation, then even when following objects and conditions, they could not arise.
Why? Because they have not been cultivated and have not been contemplated. Regarding "infants," the *Cāngjié piān* (Cangjie’s Lexicon) says: [text omitted].
The girl is called *ying* and the boy is called *hai*. When these children are young, as they pursue objects and follow conditions, they gradually develop likes and dislikes;
from this we know that they must have already practiced and contemplated these things in previous lives.

Due to being reborn and passing through successive worlds, they had forgotten their former habits, but now, because they encounter those same objects and conditions again, their likes and dislikes gradually become manifest. How could this be merely a matter of temperament? It is not so.

If one were to claim that things suddenly exist spontaneously and can thus accord with one's thoughts regarding likes and dislikes, then why could the five virtues and six arts not all be understood by mere thought;
what need would there be for them to be accomplished through the causes and conditions of study and training?

If it is claimed that [the spirit] suddenly arises and so forth—that is, if this spiritual consciousness receives its vital breath and suddenly exists naturally without prior accumulated habituation—then it would be able to follow its thoughts toward love or hatred even in states of arrogance and indulgence. Consequently, all virtues and arts could be understood at will upon thought;

for instance, upon encountering female beauty one would immediately feel desire, and upon meeting with a craft or skill one would immediately act, and upon seeing injustice one would immediately be able to sever it.
Regarding enemies and kin, one should be able to resolve matters without waiting ten or five years for the capacity to act;
since this is not the case now, we know that it is not the case that [the spirit] arises suddenly and can immediately follow thought.

Since there is no principle of spontaneous self-formation through following thought, but rather the way of transformation through conditions and practice, then when one receives the vital breath (*qi*) to form the spirit, the spirit disperses and returns to the breath.
This is not merely appropriate for the present; viewed from this perspective, it is clear that the "spiritual knowledge" (shenzhi) is not simply qi.

The five virtues are precisely the five constants (wuchang). To state the essential point: the operation of the five virtues is what is called the five phases (wuxing). Regarding "phases," Lao Dan said they are the movement of the heavenly qi.
Wood is the virtue of benevolence (ren); metal is the virtue of righteousness (yi); fire is the virtue of ritual propriety (li); and water is the virtue of trustworthiness (xin).
Regarding the virtues of Earth and Wisdom: since the Earth reigns over the four seasons, these four virtues are collectively termed "Wisdom.
Now, what is benevolence (*ren*)? It is that which means loving all things without exception. What is righteousness (*yi*)?
It is that which means acting according to what is appropriate. What is ritual propriety (*li*)? It is that which means ordering the sequence of things so that they do not lose their proper order.
What is meant by "the wise"? It refers to one who is thoroughly proficient in all matters. What is meant by "the faithful"?
It refers to one who attains what is appropriate and maintains it without loss. The Six Arts are: first, ritual; second, music;
third, archery; fourth, charioteering; fifth, calligraphy; and sixth, mathematics. "Mathematics" refers to the art of calculation, and "arts" refers to talents and abilities.
Furthermore, if birth is the sudden presence of vital energy (*qi*) received from Heaven, and death is the sudden absence of that energy as it disperses, then who are the ghosts and spirits?
As for the question of who constitutes ghosts and spirits, both the teachings of external schools and worldly people alike grant that such things exist.
Regarding this difficulty, the *Book of Documents* states: "He who possesses many talents and skills can serve the ghosts and spirits. The *Changes* (*Zhouyi*) says:
"Therefore, one knows the conditions and manifestations of ghosts and spirits.

Furthermore, there are those in the world who possess the clarity to perceive past lives and recall former events; from this, we know that the continuity of existence prior to birth is not merely a matter of inheriting vital breath (*qi*).
Yet, there were those who suddenly possessed the faculty of *jñāna* (clairvoyance), perceiving past lives and recollecting former events; "jñāna" means a mirror or a reflection.

Thus, tracing the past and continuing into the future, I have briefly recorded three individuals: first, Yang Hu (pronounced Hù), styled Shuzi, the Jin Grand Mentor (*taifu*), who at the age of five once...
He ordered his wet nurse to retrieve the ring he had previously been playing with. The wet nurse said, "You did not have this object before; where did you get it?
Xu replied, "I was playing by the eastern wall when it fell into the midst of a mulberry tree. The wet nurse said, "You should go and look for it yourself.
Xu said, "This is not my former residence; as a child, I do not know its location. Later, he went out to wander among the neighboring houses.

1. Only after providing explanations and metaphors does one then cease [the inquiry]. 2. The *Book of Jin* states that Bao Jing (pronounced Jìng), styled Taixuan, was born in Donghai.

He prayed that his parents might entrust him with their care so that he might find peace and happiness. His wife woke up in alarm and wept as she told Ji.

Yuan Ke sought their assistance to ensure victory. He questioned them, saying, "Who are you that can provide such aid?
They replied, "We are the fathers of the concubines favored by your late father’s general.

The general Du Hui was surrounded by a dense thicket of grass, with no way to advance or retreat; he was defeated by the army of Jin.
As the saying goes, "The ghosts employed the binding of grass"—this refers to this very event.
Regarding Su Zhao, the *Book of Jin* states that after Su Zhao died while serving as the Magistrate of Zhongmou, his nephew named Jie would frequently see Zhao appear and converse with him.
The speech was no different from that of a living person. Forty times in succession, when Jie came to visit, he asked, "How is death compared to life?
Yao replied, "It is no different. Jie said, "It must surely not be as good. Yao smiled and said, "You shall know this for yourself later.
Jie asked, "Why does the deceased not return to their former corpse? Yao said, "It is like cutting off one of your arms and casting it away."
When the ground was peeled away, there was no harm to you, yet the corpse remained in such a state.

thus, the cycle of the six realms has never known an end. How could it be that humans alone die while ghosts do not? If one were to live forever without dying, then what you have argued would indeed be correct.
Furthermore, the qi of heaven and earth is fundamentally without consciousness. Since humans receive this unconscious qi, how could it suddenly arise as consciousness?
How could it suddenly arise as consciousness? For consciousness is precisely the spiritual awareness (*vijñāna*); this spirit possesses the qualities of being wise or foolish, and good or evil.
The myriad differences of evil arise from the breath of ignorance; how could these thousand variations exist [without it]? Now, consciousness and breath are distinct:

Based on this, we know that it is not the case that the mind arises from qi as its fundamental substance; for if the mind were produced by qi, it could not distinguish between good and evil.

Since plants and trees also receive the vital breath (*qi*), why do they not possess knowledge?
To what extent must one reach before knowledge arises? If there were a category of beings that possesses knowledge, they would receive the breath of Yin and Yang;

Indeed, if calamity and disorder arose from Heaven and rebellion originated from Fate, then the Sage would have established his teachings to blame Heaven rather than man, and to condemn things rather than Fate; yet such is not the case. Why is this?
Because he does not seek the cause in things while blaming things, nor does he seek it in Heaven while blaming Heaven; thus, the Sage’s teaching returns [to the human realm].

Regarding the cause:

Regarding emotions such as joy and anger, the Confucians designate joy, anger, sorrow, fear, love, hate, and desire as the "seven emotions" (*qíqíng*). These arise momentarily;
"chà" (乍) means for a brief time, and "qǐ" (起) means to arise or be produced.

"Now that this body has died, who is it that experiences the retribution of suffering and joy?

Although the metaphors differ, they are identical in principle regarding the Dharma.

My own body is likewise a transformation of consciousness; due to delusion, one clings to the existence of a self and various external objects, thereby giving rise to afflictions and creating karma, leading to an endless cycle of birth and death (as explained in detail previously).
Regarding the phrase "My body is also like this": according to the preface to the *Chanyan quan*, it states, "This physical form of mine, as well as the external world, are likewise so.

That preface intends to shatter the objective realm by means of consciousness, and thus clarifies both the environment (*āśraya*) and its inhabitants (*adhiṣṭhāna*). This treatise, however, traces the origin of the body itself and manifests only the retributive reward (*vipāka*).
Therefore, it says, "My body is also like this," meaning that all objective realms are precisely what I possess (*mama-ātmīya*). For a detailed explanation, see the commentary.
As stated previously in the preceding text: "Because this self cherishes these [afflictions], even the three poisons strike the mind, inciting the body and speech to create all manner of karma.
Once karma is formed, it is difficult to escape; thus one undergoes suffering and pleasure in various bodies, cycling through birth after birth for kalpa after kalpa without end."
Only by awakening to and understanding this principle does one know that one's own body is a transformation of consciousness alone, and that consciousness is the fundamental basis of the body.
(Self-annotation: The meaning of "not understanding" will be refuted later.)

The Great Vehicle Teaching on the Shattering of Characteristics (*Mahāyāna-lakṣaṇa-bhañjana-śāsana*) shatters the teachings on the characteristics of the preceding vehicles of the Great and Small Vehicles, while secretly revealing the subsequent principle of the true nature’s emptiness and quiescence.

This Great Vehicle Teaching on the Shattering of Characteristics is identical to what is called the "Teaching that Secretly Intends to Shatter Characteristics and Reveal Nature" in the *Preface to the Exposition of Chan*.
If we follow the analogy of those three types of Buddhist teachings to verify the three schools of Chan mind, then:

the Mahāyāna Dharma-lakṣaṇa teaching verifies the school that cultivates the mind by quelling delusions; this Mahāyāna teaching of destroying marks verifies the school of ultimate extinction and non-reliance;

and the final One Vehicle teaching of revealing nature verifies the school that directly reveals the nature of mind. This [last school] refutes the lower, Hinayāna Dharma-lakṣaṇa [teaching], which holds that form is identical to emptiness.

The three poisons of the mind constitute the root of the body, the sense organs (*indriya*), and the objective world (*dhātu*). In the Mahāyāna Dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), these three objects are suddenly transformed as mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), taking the *ālayavijñāna* as their basis.
This is secretly revealed in the subsequent section on the "Commentary on the Meaning of Chan" (*Chánquánzhù*), which states:

"The intent lies in revealing the nature (*xìng*), while the words serve to shatter appearances (*xiàng*); since this intent does not manifest within the words themselves, it is called 'secret' (*mì*). This refers to the true nature (*bhūtatathatā*) which is empty and quiescent.
Regarding the Principle (the direct revelation of the true source according to the chapters; the manifestation of the nature through the One Vehicle according to the teachings):

[Self-annotation] The discourse on the shattering of characteristics is found not only in the various Prajñāpāramitā sūtras but pervades all Mahāyāna scriptures. In the first three teachings, it follows a sequential order of priority;
however, in this teaching, it shatters attachments as they arise, without fixed temporal stages.

Therefore, Nāgārjuna establishes two kinds of prajñā: the common and the uncommon. The common is that which is heard, believed, and understood by the followers of the two vehicles alike, because it destroys their attachment to the teachings of the two vehicles.
The uncommon is that which is understood exclusively by bodhisattvas, because it reveals the Buddha-nature.
Therefore, the two Indian masters Śīlabhadra and Jñānaprabha each established a system of the three-period teachings;
regarding this teaching of emptiness, some say it precedes the Vijñaptimātra-dharmalakṣaṇa [Yogācāra], while others say it follows it. Herein, our intention is to adopt the latter view.

Each established three periods, the latter being that of the Master Śīlabhadra, who inherited distantly from Maitreya and Asaṅga and followed closely upon Dharmapāla and Sthiramati, establishing three types of teaching:
first, the Teaching of Existence, namely the Āgamas and other sūtras; second, the Teaching of Emptiness, namely the various Prajñāpāramitā sūtras;
and third, the Teaching of the Middle Way, namely the Saṃdhinirmocana and other sūtras. Of these, the former two are not of definitive meaning (*neyārtha*).

On the other hand, the master of definitive meaning, Jñānaprabha, who inherited the lineage of Mañjuśrī and Nāgārjuna from afar and received the teachings of Viśuddhasimha and Bhāviveka more recently, also established a system of three periods of teaching:
first, at the Deer Park, he taught the Hīnayāna, wherein both object and mind exist;

second, he taught the Mahāyāna of the Dharma-characteristics (lakṣaṇa), wherein the object is empty but the mind exists; and finally, he taught the Mahāyāna of signlessness (animitta), wherein both object and mind are empty. Furthermore...

The former two are not of definitive meaning (*neyārtha*), while the latter one is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Regarding the period [of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] within the Dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*), some say it was prior to the master Śīlabhadra, while others say it was subsequent to the master Jñānaprabha.
When one wishes to refute this, one first interrogates them, saying: "If the objects that are transformed are illusory, how could the consciousness that performs the transformation be real?

Since the objects that are transformed are illusory—as the *Yuanjue chao* (Commentary on Perfect Enlightenment) illustrates with the metaphor of the butterfly's form being entirely empty and non-existent—how could the perception of the butterfly be anything other than non-existent as well?"
If one were to say that one exists while the other does not,
then the dream-image and the object seen therein would necessarily be distinct.
For example, when Zhuang Zhou was asleep, he dreamed that his body had become a butterfly, fluttering about in a flower garden.
If they were different, then the dream would not be the object and the object would not be the dream; yet when one awakens and the dream ceases, that object ought to remain.
As for "the dream is not the object and the object is not the dream," it is like saying the dream is not the butterfly and the butterfly is also not the dream;

yet when one awakens and the dream ceases, that object ought to remain. One should say that when one awakens and the dream ceases, the butterfly ought to remain—this is because [the two are distinct].
This is because objects are distinguished as real or false.
Furthermore, if an object were not a dream, it would have to be a real object; if a dream were not an object, by what could its characteristics be defined?
Moreover, in the four lines below concerning "objects," one should simply read the character for "object" (物) as the character for "butterfly" (蝶); thus, the analogy will be clearly established.

Thus we know that during a dream, one dreams of objects; although there appears to be a distinction between the seer and the seen, according to principle they are both equally false and utterly non-existent.
Therefore, the passage below should state: "The distinction between the seer and the seen is like that between dreaming and being a butterfly."
They are, in reality, one essence.
*Yuanren lun fami lu*, Part Two;
*Yuanren lun fami lu*, Part Three.
The various consciousnesses are likewise so, for they all depend upon a multitude of conditions and lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Thus, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* states: "There has never been a single phenomenon that does not arise from causes and conditions;

therefore, there is no phenomenon that is not empty. It further states: "Phenomena produced by causes and conditions—I declare them to be emptiness. (From the *Bodhisattva-bhūmi* of the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*)
It is said: "All dharmas exist only through the differentiation of deluded thought;
if one is free from mental ideation, then there are no signs of any objective realms. As the Sūtra states: "Whatever has marks is entirely false and illusory;
to be free from all marks is what is called the Buddhas. (Passages such as these are found throughout the Mahāyāna canon.)
Thus we know that the emptiness of both mind and objects is precisely the true principle of the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the phrase "precisely the true principle of the Mahāyāna," this first grants [the opponent's position] as the true principle of "mere emptiness" (but-śūnyatā);
the meaning of its inadequacy will be refuted later in the text.

If, according to this original body, the very source of the body is originally emptiness and that emptiness is itself the fundamental reality, one might now further challenge this teaching by asking: "If both mind and objects are non-existent, who is it that knows?"
"Who is it that knows there is nothing?"—this single phrase comes from the letter of the King of Qin. He said:

"The various schools all claim to penetrate the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), asserting that it is vast, empty, and quiescent, such that no Sage exists. If there is no Sage, who is it that knows there is nothing?
Now, the Master of the Treatise borrows the force of these words to refute the view that both mind and objects are non-existent.
Furthermore, if there were no real dharmas at all, upon what could these various false appearances depend?
Moreover, we observe in the world that no false object ever arises without depending on a real dharma.
Just as there can be no waves of false and provisional appearance without water that is unchanging and devoid of moisture,
how could there be various false and provisional reflections without a mirror that is pure, luminous, and unchanging?
Just as water that is not low-lying or damp and a mirror of pure clarity are both metaphors for the primordially existing, intrinsically pure true mind.
Furthermore, as for the previous statement that dream appearances and dream objects are equally illusory, it is indeed as you have said.
However, this illusory dream must necessarily depend on a sleeping person;
since it necessarily depends on a sleeping person, the intrinsically pure true mind is likewise identical to the original mind of Zhuang Zhou while he was asleep.
Now that both mind and objects are seen to be empty, I do not yet understand upon what basis these delusive appearances manifest.
Therefore, I know that this teaching merely destroys clinging attachments, yet it has not yet clearly revealed the nature of the true spirit.
Therefore, the *Dharmabherī-sūtra* states that all sūtras on emptiness are "provisional teachings" (the term "provisional" meaning that further meanings remain unelucidated),
while the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states that emptiness is the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna.
These four preceding teachings, viewed in relation to one another, are progressively shallower before and deeper after.

They are progressively shallower before and deeper after because the Human and Celestial Teaching is limited to karmic retribution; the Śrāvaka (Small Vehicle) Teaching is limited to the coarse characteristics of the latter four [realms];
the Teaching of Characteristics is limited to the three subtle [realms]; and the Teaching of Destroying Characteristics secretly reveals the true nature. Thus, the Human and Celestial...

The "Shallow" refers to the teaching that refutes characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vibhaṅga*), and the "Profound" refers to the teaching of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Regarding the two intermediate teachings, their relative shallowness and profundity are discussed in mutual relation: viewed from the perspective of what precedes them, they are profound; viewed from the perspective of what follows them, they are shallow.

If one merely practices them and knows for oneself that they are not yet fully understood, this is termed "shallow. If one clings to them as being fully understood, this is termed "partial" (*ekāntika*).
Therefore, those who study this tradition say it is partial and shallow.
Third, "Truly Revealing the True Source":

the single character "source" (*yuan*) is a metaphor for the original enlightened nature (*benjue zhenxing*) inherent in all sentient beings; within the myriad phenomena, it serves as their foundation.
The source of correctness lies in sentient beings as the source of delusion and awakening; in Bodhisattvas, it is the source of the myriad practices;
and in the Buddhas, it is the source of the myriad virtues.

The One Vehicle Teaching that Reveals Nature (*Ekayāna-prakṛti-vyakti-śāsana*) states that all sentient beings possess the fundamentally awakened true mind (*mūla-bodhi-satya-citta*), which is beginningless.

That which has been eternally present since time immemorial— pure, luminous, unclouded, and characterized by constant, clear awareness— is called Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) and is also called the Tathāgatagarbha.
This teaching of the One Vehicle that reveals nature is identical to the teaching on the true mind as being nature itself, as demonstrated in the "Preface to the Exposition of Chan."
Because the Chan school is the school that directly reveals the nature of the mind, it is said to be "identical with nature" (*jìngxìng*).

This transcends the third [stage], the Dharma-characteristics (*fǎxiàng*) school, and the fourth, the Refutation of Characteristics (*pòxiàng*) school; therefore, it is said to "reveal nature. Furthermore, because it differs from the partial and shallow aspects of the Mahāyāna, it is designated as the "One Vehicle" (*ekayāna*).

(The Mahāyāna Dharma-characteristics school resides in the gate of birth-and-death and culminates in the three subtle states; the Mahāyāna Refutation of Characteristics school resides in the gate of True Suchness and secretly reveals the meaning of emptiness—both are partial and shallow. Regarding the phrase "explaining all," this refers to the gate of Truth (*zhēn*).
Just as the nature [of things] pervades all sentient beings, so too does the fundamentally enlightened true mind exist within them all. The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"The Dharma-nature pervades all places—within all sentient beings and throughout all lands. The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states: "White stone possesses the nature of silver;
yellow stone possesses the nature of gold; likewise, all sentient beings possess the nature of nirvāṇa. These are all excellent proofs of this point.

Regarding that which has been eternally abiding and pure since beginningless time, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "All sentient beings are fundamentally and eternally abiding," and further states: "It is neither lost nor destroyed; it is the eternally abiding single mind.

Because from the very beginning it has never been associated with any defiled dharmas, it is called 'pure. Now, this purity possesses two meanings, as stated in the *Anuttaraśraya-sūtra*: I. Innate Purity (*prakṛti-vyavadāna*) II. Purity through Cultivation (*vaimalya-vyavadāna*) The first refers to the fact that the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha is inherently pure, free from all adventitious defilements. The second refers to the state where, by relying on the power of the Mahāyāna teachings, one removes all afflictions and realizes the original purity. These two purities correspond respectively to the "fundamental purity" and the "purity resulting from the removal of stains" mentioned in the *Awakening of Faith*. Thus, while the essence of the mind is primordially pure, it is only through the cultivation of the path that this innate purity is fully manifested.

It is said that the first is intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*), which is its universal characteristic; the second is purity through the removal of stains (*vaimalya-viśuddhi*), which is its specific characteristic.
In the *Ratnagotravibhāga* there are likewise two meanings: first, intrinsic purity, which refers to liberation by nature (*prakṛti-vimukti*);
second, purity through the removal of stains, which refers to liberation from obstructions (*vimala-vimukti*). What is here termed "everlasting purity" is the universal [characteristic].

The nature of characteristics is the pure liberation. That which is luminously clear, not obscure, and always known is explained in the "Chapter on Dedication" (*Parindāna-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*:
because True Suchness (*tathatā*) has illumination as its nature, it is said to be "not obscure. This term "knowing" does not refer to cognitive realization;
rather, it means that the true nature is distinct from empty space or wood and stone, and thus it is called "knowing. It is not like the cognition of an object through conditions.

The consciousness of discrimination is not like the wisdom that thoroughly comprehends through its illuminating essence; rather, it is the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*) itself, which possesses natural and constant knowing.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa stated: "True Suchness is the meaning of self-essence, reality, and cognitive awareness.
It is also called Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), for it is the source of the myriad virtues of all Buddhas; thus, it is named Buddha-nature. It is the multitude... [text ends]

Because it is the source from which both delusion and awakening arise, it is called the *Tathāgatagarbha* (the Womb of the Tathāgata). [This interpretation of the preceding text’s meaning relies largely on the terminology of Chan, while also incorporating the doctrinal principles of Xianshou].

From the beginningless past, it has been obscured by the cataracts of false conceptualization; thus, one fails to realize its true nature and merely identifies with the ordinary physical body. Consequently, one becomes attached to karmic bonds and undergoes the suffering of birth and death.
"From the beginningless limit, it is the limit of being obscured by the cataracts of false imagination; 'obscured' means hindered. False imagination is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*).
As stated in the *Awakening of Faith*: 'From time beginningless, all are due to being perfumed by ignorance.

Furthermore, the meaning of the defiled mind is termed the 'hindrance of affliction' (*kleśāvaraṇa*), because it can obstruct the fundamental wisdom of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Therefore, one does not spontaneously realize or know [it]."
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "True bliss is inherently present, yet one loses it through ignorance; delusory suffering is inherently empty, yet one attains it without realization.
To merely recognize the downward-tending [mind] as manifesting false thoughts is the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), which is the cognitive hindrance (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*).

To merely recognize the ordinary physical substance as the self is the attachment to the self (*ātma-grāha*), which is the afflictive hindrance (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*). To be addicted to and bound by karma and its retribution is the karmic hindrance (*karma-āvaraṇa*), whereby one undergoes birth and death."
Suffering is itself an obstacle to retribution.

Out of compassion for them, the Great Awakened One taught that all things are empty, and further revealed that the true mind of spiritual awakening is pure and entirely identical to that of all Buddhas.

Since the Great Awakened One (*Mahābodhi*) is the World-Honored One (*Bhagavān*), the preface states: "To respond with immediate penetration is called the Great Awakened Honored One; it is compassion.
The statement that "all is empty" means that both the mundane cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) and the supramundane *nirvāṇa* are all empty;

this describes the preceding section on the refutation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). "Revealing the numinous awakening" and below correctly describe the manifestation of the nature (*prakṛti*); this is the "Questioning and Clarifying Chapter."
Regarding the statement that "their nature is fundamentally pure and reveals that all sentient beings are entirely identical to all Buddhas," the *Qingliang shu* (Cool Grove Commentary) states:
"All living beings without exception contain Buddha-wisdom; the perfect and universal Dharma is fully present in them."
Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "O Son of the Buddha, there is not a single sentient being who does not possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata;

it is only because of deluded thoughts and attachments that they do not realize it. If one is free from deluded thoughts, then all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*), spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhūjñāna*), and unimpeded wisdom (*asaṅgajñāna*) will immediately manifest before them."
Therefore, in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, these all appear in the "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Causes of Sentient Beings. Regarding the phrase "merely by means of," the full text says:

"merely by means of deluded thoughts, inverted views, and attachment. The commentary explains: "The 'deluded thoughts' of ordinary beings and the 'attachment and inverted views' of those of provisional [Hīnayāna] and small [Mahāyāna] capacities apply to both."
He then cites the analogy of a single mote of dust containing a scripture scroll as vast as the great trichiliocosm;
the mote represents sentient beings, while the scripture represents the Buddha’s wisdom. He further cites the passage from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* (the "Great Scripture") which states:

"Suppose there were a great scripture scroll (representing the Buddha’s wisdom) equal in size to the great trichiliocosm (its essence being boundless and pervading the entire Dharma-realm), upon which were inscribed all the events of the great trichiliocosm."
All are completely exhausted (this metaphorically represents that the body originally possesses sands-of-the-Ganges virtues and sands-of-the-Ganges wondrous functions).

Although this great scripture is as vast in measure as the Great Trichiliocosm, it dwells entirely within a single minute atom (this metaphor represents that the Buddha-wisdom is fully present and perfectly complete within the bodies of sentient beings).
Just as with this one atom (taking one sentient being as an example), all atoms are likewise so; therefore, it says, "An atom illustrates the multitude."
Thus it was born.
Subsequently, it further states: "At that time, the Tathāgata surveyed all sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm and spoke these words:
'How marvelous, how marvelous! Why is it that these sentient beings, though possessing the wisdom of the Tathāgata, are deluded and do not see it?'"

I shall instruct them with the Noble Path so that they may forever leave behind deluded thoughts and, within their own bodies, perceive the vast wisdom of the Tathāgata, which is no different from that of the Buddha.
"Instructing them with the Noble Path" means teaching those sentient beings to cultivate the Noble Path, which is the cause for the path; this refers to the six [perfections].
The *pāramitās* are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).

The critique states: "For many kalpas we have not encountered the True Dharma; failing to understand it, we instead seek its origin within our own bodies, yet cling only to illusory appearances, content to identify ourselves as mere ordinary beings, whether as animals or humans."
The evaluation is indeed correct: the True Sect (Shinshū) is simply Buddhism;

however, it adheres to the *Awakening of Faith* by stating that one falsely takes the four elements to be the appearance of one's own body and the shadows of the six sense-objects to be the appearance of one's own mind. Therefore, it concludes by saying, "To willingly acknowledge oneself as an ordinary person of the lower class."
Now, tracing back to the ultimate teaching, one realizes that one’s original nature is that of a Buddha.

"Ultimate teaching" refers to the most profound discourse of the Buddha, namely the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Regarding "original nature is that of a Buddha," the *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* states:
"The mind is originally the Buddha; it is through the arising of thought that drifting and sinking appear. Furthermore, the "Manifestation Chapter" (*Prakāśa-parivarta*) says: "As..."
One knows that sentient beings have been Buddhas from the very beginning.
Therefore, one must practice in accordance with the Buddha’s conduct and align the mind with the Buddha’s mind. Returning to the root and source, one severs ordinary habits;
diminishing them further and further until reaching the state of non-action (*wuwei*). When their spontaneous application is as vast as the sands of the Ganges, this is called "Buddha."
Therefore, the *Qingliang xinyao* states: "If one allows quiescent awareness to proceed spontaneously, then all practices will arise;

this is for practice to accord with the Buddha's practice. If one is without-mind and forgets even illumination, then all myriad burdens are eliminated; this is for the mind to coincide with the Buddha's mind.
Regarding "returning to the root and returning to the source," the *Dasu* (Great Commentary) states: "It causes all sentient beings to return to the root and return to the source."
Tracing its source back to the limit of the future, it never ceases; all that is practiced is the habit-energy of an ordinary person.
To diminish this is to take it as the Way. Daily diminishing is the reduction of delusions; daily learning is the increase of wisdom.

When one diminishes again and again until there is nothing left to diminish, then tranquil illumination manifests before one, and one naturally responds to the needs of beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—what else could this be but the Buddha?
One should know that delusion and awakening are one and the same true mind. How magnificent! This wondrous gate brings the original person to this point.
Regarding "delusion and awakening are one and the same true mind": delusion refers to sentient beings, while awakening refers to the Buddhas.

As a Great Sūtra states, "Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction"; therefore, they are said to be one and the same. "How magnificent! is an expression of reverent praise.
The term "wondrous gate" (*miaomen*) is a designation for that which transcends thought.
(Self-note: However, the Buddha taught the first five teachings as being either gradual or sudden.
Regarding these terms "gradual" or "sudden," the *Xuanxu* (Explanatory Preface) states: "Transforming the ordinary into the sagely is 'gradual'; awakening from delusion is 'sudden.'"

Sudden. If there are those of middling or inferior capacity, they are guided and received gradually from the shallow to the profound: first, the initial teaching is expounded to cause them to leave evil and abide in good;

next, the second and third teachings are expounded to cause them to leave defilement and abide in purity; finally, the fourth and fifth teachings are discussed to shatter appearances and reveal reality.
By nature, the provisional ultimately returns to the real; relying on the teaching of reality, one practices until attaining Buddhahood.

For those of middling and inferior capacities, the general approach involves gradual cultivation and gradual awakening to clarify how the middling and inferior leave evil and abide in good—this refers to the teachings for humans and devas that involve leaving the ten unwholesome acts and practicing the ten wholesome ones—and how they leave defilement and abide in purity, which in the case of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) means leaving [defilement].

The pure dharma-characteristic of dwelling in the emptiness of self amidst the defilement of afflictions is precisely the departure from the defilement of the knowable and the dwelling in the purity of the emptiness of dharmas;
the convergence of the provisional upon the real is precisely the convergence of the provisional that destroys appearances upon the real that reveals the nature.

If one possesses the wisdom of the highest of the high faculties, then from beginning to end—meaning from the outset—one relies upon the fifth [gate], which directly points to the essence of the single true mind.
Once the essence of the mind is revealed, one realizes for oneself that everything is entirely illusory and originally empty and quiescent.

It is only because of delusion that one relies on the True and gives rise to the semblance; therefore, one must employ the wisdom that awakens to the Truth to sever evil and cultivate good, ceasing delusion and returning to the True.
When delusion is exhausted and the true is perfected, this is called the Dharma-body Buddha.
If one of the highest faculties reaches the state where wisdom is fundamentally empty and quiescent, this is sudden enlightenment (*tunwu*).

The passage from "It is simply because of delusion" onwards concerns gradual cultivation (*jianxiu*). Because one is deluded by ignorance, it becomes false affliction; by awakening to these false afflictions as [delusion],...
True wisdom is the wisdom that awakens to reality; it is the capacity to sever the evil of delusive confusion, which is that which is severed. The remainder is as stated in the text.
Section Four: Harmonizing the Fundamental and the Derivative (harmonizing what was previously refuted so that they all return to a single source, establishing them all as the correct teaching).

Regarding the "synthesis of the fundamental and the derivative": the derivative refers to the first [section], which refutes deluded attachments, and the second, which refutes partiality and shallowness;
the fundamental refers to the third, which directly reveals the true source. Therefore, it is said that what was previously refuted is synthesized and returns to a single source.
Although true nature (*tathatā*) is the fundamental basis of the body, its arising must have a cause; it cannot suddenly manifest as the form of a body without reason.

"Although true nature is the fundamental basis of the body" refers to the preceding teaching on the manifestation of nature, which states that all sentient beings possess the fundamentally awakened true mind (*mūla-bodhi-citta*).
"Its arising must have a cause" means that the delusion of the true leads to the production of the deluded mind.

Because there is a cause, faith arises; it is said that failing to know the Dharma of True Suchness (*tathatā*) as it truly is, the single mind of non-awakening (*abodha*) arises—this is the source from which delusion originates.
One must not fail to understand that the "body" refers to the root-body manifested within the phenomenal realm, which is the body-form suddenly formed.
However, because the preceding tenets were not yet fully understood, they are refuted point by point.
From the "Preceding Tenets" section below, beginning with the "Deluded Attachment Tenet" and ending with the "Refutation of Characteristics Tenet," there are five sections.

Now, I shall synthesize the beginning and the end; even the teachings of Confucianism and Daoism are included (initially only the fifth nature is taught therein, but from the subsequent sections onward, the stages of progression become identical to those of the various other teachings, each as noted in the annotations).
This refers to the single, primordial, true spiritual nature.
As it says in the *Awakening of Faith*: "That which is called the Dharma is the mind of sentient beings. "All" refers to the four noble ones;
"beings" refers to the six classes of ordinary beings. The *Preface* states: "The fundamental root of both ordinary beings and sages is entirely this numinous, pure, and luminous oneness."

The mind of the dharma-realm (which is identical to the true, singular spiritual nature described in this text) is neither born nor extinguished, neither increases nor decreases, and neither changes nor alters.
It does not give rise to birth; thus it is said in the *Awakening of Faith*: "That which is called the nature of the mind is neither born nor extinguished, and possesses no variation."
Reaching the realm beyond thought is accessible only through direct realization (the preceding section merely summarizes and introduces the treatise, or cites the *Chanxuan xu* as proof).
Because sentient beings have been mired in beginningless delusion and sleep, failing to awaken to their own nature, it is concealed and thus called the *Tathāgatagarbha*.

'lost' is a metaphor for ignorance (*avidyā*), and 'directions' is a metaphor for the nature of awakening. If one follows the preceding text, it says: "Thus, this dream of false construction..."

It must be because of a sleeping person that sleep is used as a metaphor for the awakened nature (*jñāna*) and dreams as a metaphor for deluded consciousness; both belong to the gate of arising and ceasing.

The commentary is likewise [as follows]: below, it should state, "likewise identical to the refutation of these existing marks of arising and ceasing," for these marks are precisely the defilement and purity, increase and decrease.
Thus, the *Heart Sūtra* says: "The empty characteristic of all dharmas is neither born nor extinguished..."
The impurities and lack of purity neither increase nor decrease, being exactly like this. That which is called the true mind,
which is neither born nor extinguished, in conjunction with the deluded thoughts of birth and extinction— being neither identical nor different—
is termed the *ālayavijñāna*.
What is called "arising from below" in the *Awakening of Faith* refers to the union of the unborn and undying with the birth-and-death [phenomena].

What is now called the "true mind" is precisely the unborn and undying Tathāgatagarbha, while "delusive thought" is the mind characterized by birth-and-death. Thus, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"The True alone does not arise; delusion alone cannot be established; it is only through the union of the True and the delusive that there is anything produced."

The second is the "phase of the capacity to see," which means that because it relies on movement, the capacity to see arises; this refers here to the transformation into the consciousness that is capable of seeing.

The third is the "phase of objective realms," which means that because it relies on the capacity to see, objective realms falsely appear; this refers here to the manifestation of the phase of objective realms.

"Spontaneous suchness" means that things are not made so by any external agent.

Alas! How lamentable that those with meager learning hold such diverse and chaotic attachments.

"Fenran" (紛然) describes a state of disorder. Taken together, this refers to those of little learning who harbor heterodox views and groundless attachments in a state of total confusion.
Because of this confusion, Master Zao said, "The discourses of heterodox schools have been in disarray for a long time. Or it may be that he was saying this to Tonghui:
"I am truly ashamed of my meager learning and my empty old age. These were merely the humble words of a minister addressing the Son of Heaven.
I address you, O practitioners of the Way: those who wish to attain Buddhahood must thoroughly penetrate both the coarse and the subtle, as well as the fundamental and the derivative;
only then can they abandon the derivative to return to the fundamental and reflect back upon the source of the mind.

I address you, O practitioners of the Way—that is, those who study the Way—there is nothing beyond this. Furthermore, these words are entrusted to future sages; it is only fitting that they act accordingly.

Regarding the "medium" [level], the coarse and subtle aspects are distinguished according to the sequence of delusions in the following text. Regarding the "fundamental and derivative" in terms of the teachings:

this means abandoning the derivative ends of the first two sections to return to the fundamental source that directly reveals the truth; thus it is said, "transforming the illumination to reach the source of the mind."

When the coarse is exhausted and the subtle is eliminated, the numinous nature manifests; there is nothing it does not penetrate, which is called the Dharma-Body (Dharmakāya). Its spontaneous and inexhaustible manifestation is called the Transformation-Buddha (Nirmāṇakāya).

"The exhaustion of the coarse and elimination of the subtle" refers to the two types of awakening—the initial arising of faith and the ultimate realization according to one's capacity—as stated in the *Awakening of Faith*: "Contemplation without abiding in signs."
Because it is free from the characteristics of coarse conceptualization, it is called "partial awakening" (*prādeśika-bodhi*).

Furthermore, it is said that because the mind’s initial arising is realized as having no initial characteristic, and because it is far removed from subtle conceptualization, it is called "ultimate awakening" (*atyanta-bodhi*).
Since the numinous nature is the *dharmakāya*, the treatise states: "The *dharmakāya* manifests spontaneously, possessing inconceivable karma and various functions."
Therefore, it is said that there is no dharma to which [the Buddha] does not penetrate. The Dharma-body is principle (*li*), and the Reward-body is wisdom (*zhi*);

when principle and wisdom are merged in profound harmony, like a pearl and its radiance, the transformative function is immediately manifested. Thus, it is said that his responsive manifestations are inexhaustible.
